#Definitions of data science

.pull-left[
## What is data science?

> "Data science is an **interdisciplinary academic field** that uses statistics, scientific computing, scientific methods, processes, algorithms and systems to extract or extrapolate knowledge and insights from potentially noisy, structured, or unstructured data." - [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_science)

> "Data science is a concept to **unify statistics, data analysis, informatics**, and their related methods to understand and analyze actual phenomena with data." - [Chikio Hayashi](https://www.springer.com/book/9784431702085) 

> "Data science encompasses a **set of principles**, problem definitions, algorithms, and processes for **extracting nonobvious and useful patterns from large data sets**." - [John Kelleher and Brendan Tierney](https://mrce.in/ebooks/Data%20Science.pdf)
]

--

# The COMPAS algorithm to predict criminals' recidivism

.pull-left[
## Background

- Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions (COMPAS) is a decision support tool developed by Northpointe (now Equivant) used by U.S. courts to **assess the likelihood of recidivism**
- Produced several scales (Pretrial release risk, General recidivism, Violent recidivism) based on factors such as age, criminal history, and substance abuse
- The algorithm is proprietary and its inner workings are not public

<br>

`Source` [Practitioner's Guide to COMPAS Core](https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/2840784/Practitioner-s-Guide-to-COMPAS-Core.pdf)
]

.pull-right[
<div align="center">
<img src="pics/compas-practitioner-1.png" width=450>
<img src="pics/compas-practitioner-2.png" width=450>
<img src="pics/compas-practitioner-3.png" width=450>
</div>
]


---
# The COMPAS algorithm to predict criminals' recidivism

.pull-left[
## The ProPublica and other investigations

- In 2016, ProPublica published an investigation showing that COMPAS was **biased against African Americans**
- **Bias:** The algorithm was more likely for African Americans to wrongly predict that defendants would re-offend.
- **Accuracy:** only 20% of people predicted to commit violent crimes actually went on to do so (in a later study estimated with 65%, still worse than a group of humans with little expertise)

<br><br><br>
`Source` [ProPublica 2016](https://www.propublica.org/article/how-we-analyzed-the-compas-recidivism-algorithm)
]

.pull-right[
<div align="center">
<img src="pics/machine-bias-compas.png" width=450>
</div>
]

# Types of data-driven research and their role for policy

.pull-left-small2[
## 1. Description
- What is the state of the world?
- What are the trends over time?
- What are the differences between groups?

## The value for policy-making
- At the center of **monitoring**
- "How many people consume misinformation online?"
- "How many people are unemployed in a certain district?"
- "How does the distribution of income vary across educational segments of the population?"
]

--

.pull-left-small2[
## 2. Explanation
- What is the effect of a policy?
- Does the effect vary across groups?
- What are the mechanisms behind the effect?

## The value for policy-making
- At the center of **evaluation**
- "Did the wage increase lead to a decrease in employment?"
- "Did the campaign affect the exposure to misinformation differently across groups?"
- "Why did the intervention not lead to the expected results?"
]

--

.pull-left-small2[
## 3. Prediction
- What is the path of an indicator?
- (When) will future events happen?
- What class does this observation most likely belong to?


## The value for policy-making
- At the center of **forecasting** but also **targeting** and **measurement**
- "Will there be conflict?"
- "How many people will be unemployed in a certain district next year?"
- "Which individuals are most likely to be affected by a policy?"
]

# Assignments and grading

| Component                           | Weight |
|:-|-:|
| 3(4) × homework assignments | pass/fail |
| 8(10) × onsite quizzes (3% each) | 24% |
| 1 × hackathon project       | 36% |
| 1 × in-class coding exam 	| 40% |

--

### Homework assignments 
- Your incentive to practice what you learn in class regularly!
- Each assignment is a mix of practical problems that are to be solved with R.
- There will be 4 assignments (one every ~2 weeks), and you'll have to submit 3 of them to pass the course.
- You'll have about one week to work on each assignment (deadline: Fridays the following week at 6pm).
- The assignments are distributed via [Classroom 50](https://classroom50.org/).
- You are encouraged to collaborate, but everyone will hand in a separate solution.
- You submit your solutions via GitHub.
- Grading: pass/fail + feedback. Your solutions don't have to be perfect, but we want to see an individual effort.


---
# Assignments and grading

| Component                           | Weight |
|:-|-:|
| 3(4) × homework assignments | pass/fail |
| 8(10) × onsite quizzes (3% each) | 24% |
| 1 × hackathon project       | 36% |
| 1 × in-class coding exam 	| 40% |

### Onsite quizzes
- The short 5-minute quizzes, administered at the beginning of the lecture, will test your knowledge about the topics covered in class. Content can be drawn from the lecture of the past week and the readings of the current.
- There will be 10 quizzes and the 8 best will contribute to the final grade.
- The quiz format will be single choice.
- You cannot make up for missed quizzes. If you miss a quiz, it will be counted as one of the two lowest scores that are dropped.
- Taking the quiz counts as attendance for the lecture. If you miss a quiz, you will be marked absent for that lecture.
- Important: Keep a pen ✎ ready for the quiz!

# Attendance

## General rules

- You cannot miss more than two sessions. If you have to miss a session for medical reasons or personal emergencies, please **inform Examination Office** and they will inform me about your absence.
- I **don't want you to notify me about absences** in advance or ex post.
- We will check attendance on-site through the quizzes.


## Office hours and advice

- If you want to discuss content from class, first do so with your Lab TA. 
- If you want to discuss something with the entire group, use the Moodle forum.
- If you want to discuss something with me, please sign up for a slot in my office hours (link on Moodle). If my office hours don't work for you, please email me and we will find a time that works for both of us.
- For general methods advice, the [Research Consulting Team at the Data Science Lab](https://hertie-data-science-lab.github.io/research-consulting/) is there for you.

# Why R and RStudio?

### Data science positivism

- Alongside Python, R has become the *de facto* language for data science.
  - See: [*The Impressive Growth of R*](https://stackoverflow.blog/2017/10/10/impressive-growth-r/), [*The Popularity of Data Science Software*](http://r4stats.com/articles/popularity/)
- Open-source (free!) with a global user-base spanning academia and industry.
  - "Do you want to be a profit source or a cost center?"

--

### Bridge to multiple other programming environments, with statistics at heart

- Already has all of the statistics support, and is amazingly adaptable as a “glue” language to other
programming languages and APIs.
- The RStudio IDE and ecosystem allow for further, seemless integration.

--

### Path dependency

- It's also the language that I know best.
- (Learning multiple languages is a good idea, though.)



---
# Why R and RStudio? (cont.)

```{R, indeeddotcom, echo = F, fig.height = 5.5, fig.width = 11, dev = "svg", warning = F, message = F}
# The popularity data: job posting counts from the Adzuna API (Germany index);
# used to be de.indeed.com, which does not provide precise counts anymore
languages <- c("Python", "SQL", "R", "SAS", "Matlab", "Julia", "SPSS", "Stata")
free_lang <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
cache_file <- "adzuna_job_counts.csv"

fetch_adzuna_count <- function(lang, app_id, app_key, attempts = 3) {
  Sys.sleep(0.5) # be gentle; rapid bursts trigger transient 503s
  url <- sprintf(
    "https://api.adzuna.com/v1/api/jobs/de/search/1?app_id=%s&app_key=%s&what=%s&results_per_page=1",
    app_id, app_key, URLencode(paste(tolower(lang), "data"))
  )
  for (i in seq_len(attempts)) {
    count <- try(jsonlite::fromJSON(url)$count, silent = TRUE)
    if (!inherits(count, "try-error")) return(count)
    Sys.sleep(2)
  }
  stop("Adzuna API request failed for ", lang)
}

pop_df <- NULL
if (file.exists(cache_file)) { # use cached counts; delete the file to force a fresh fetch
  pop_df <- read_csv(cache_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
} else {
  try({ # fetch fresh counts; requires ADZUNA_ID and ADZUNA_KEY from the key file
    load("/Users/s.munzert/rkeys.RDa")
    pop_df <- tibble(
      lang = languages,
      n_jobs = map_dbl(languages, fetch_adzuna_count, app_id = ADZUNA_ID, app_key = ADZUNA_KEY),
      free = free_lang,
      date = Sys.Date()
    )
    write_csv(pop_df, cache_file)
  }, silent = TRUE)
}
if (!is.null(pop_df)) {
  fig_subtitle <- paste0("Number of job postings for '<language> data' on adzuna.com (Germany), ", format(max(pop_df$date), "%Y/%m/%d"))
} else { # last resort: hardcoded values from the old indeed.com series
  pop_df <- tibble(
    lang = languages,
    n_jobs = c(6850, 6136, 4384, 551, 537, 249, 110, 60), # 2023/09/01
    free = free_lang
  )
  fig_subtitle <- "Number of job postings for '<language> data' on de.indeed.com, 2023/09/01"
}

## Plot it
pop_df %>%
  mutate(lang = lang %>% factor(ordered = T)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = lang, y = n_jobs, fill = free)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  aes(x = reorder(lang, -n_jobs), fill = reorder(free, -free)) +
  xlab("Statistical language") +
  scale_y_continuous(label = scales::comma) +
  ylab("Number of jobs") +
  labs(
    title = "Comparing statistical languages",
    subtitle = fig_subtitle
    ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    "Free of charge?",
    labels = c("True", "False"),
    values = c("#f92672", "darkslategray")
    ) +
  ggthemes::theme_pander(base_size = 17) +
  # theme_ipsum() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

# A detour: a brief history of the autopilot

.pull-left-wide[

### 1912-1914: The gyroscopic autopilot

- The Sperry Corporation develops the first aircraft autopilot: two gyroscopes hooked up to hydraulically operated elevators and rudder, keeping the plane straight and level.
- In 1914, Lawrence Sperry famously demonstrates the system at a flight safety competition in Paris — flying past the judges with his hands off the controls, while his mechanic walked out onto the wing.

### 1933: Around the world with "Mechanical Mike"

- Wiley Post flies solo around the world in 7 days and 19 hours in the *Winnie Mae* — a feat considered impossible for a single pilot.
- His secret: a Sperry gyroscopic autopilot (nicknamed "Mechanical Mike") and a radio direction finder effectively replaced the human navigator and let him rest during long legs.

`Image credit` Lawrence Sperry ([Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:LawrenceSperry.jpg))
]

# A brief history of the autopilot (cont.)

.pull-left-wide[

### 1947: Crossing the Atlantic hands-off

- A U.S. Air Force Douglas C-54 Skymaster crosses the Atlantic entirely under automatic control — including takeoff and landing.
- The demonstration shows that, in principle, a machine could handle a complete flight. That was almost 80 years ago!

### 1960s-today: Autoland, fly-by-wire, flight management

- 1965: First automatic landings with passengers on board in commercial service (autoland).
- 1980s onwards: Digital fly-by-wire and Flight Management Systems (FMS) turn the autopilot into an integrated flight guidance computer; modern autoland systems can touch down in almost zero visibility.
- And yet: two highly trained pilots still sit in the front of every commercial jet.

`Credit` [U.S. Air Force/Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Douglas_C-54_Skymaster_USAF.JPG), [New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/1947/09/23/archives/robotpiloted-plane-makes-safe-crossing-of-atlantic-no-hand-on.html)
]

# How modern autopilots work

.pull-left-wide[

### The system

- Modern autopilots control the aircraft around all three axes (roll, pitch, yaw), plus engine thrust (autothrottle).
- Pilots program the route into the FMS; the autopilot then tracks the lateral and vertical flight profile.
- Position and attitude come from fusing many sensors — inertial units, GPS, radio beacons — with (data science alert!) [Kalman filters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalman_filter).

### Autopilot vs. human

- The autopilot does not "think" — it executes pre-programmed control laws within a narrow envelope.
- It handles climb, cruise, descent, and (some) landings. Takeoffs? Taxiing? Unexpected situations? Still the humans' job.
- Pilots act as "automation managers": they select modes, monitor the system, and take over when it quits.
]

# Why do human pilots still exist?

.pull-left-wide[

### The training pipeline of an airline pilot

- Private license `r fa("arrow-right")` commercial license `r fa("arrow-right")` airline transport pilot (ATP) certificate.
- In the US, the ATP requires **1,500 hours of flight time** before you may fly for an airline as captain or first officer.
- Add a **type rating** for every jet you fly, plus **recurrent simulator checks** every 6-12 months — for your entire career, including practicing engine failures, stalls, and, yes, autopilot malfunctions.

### Why all this, if the autopilot flies the plane?

- Automation fails rarely, but when it does, it tends to hand over a plane that is already in trouble. The human is the redundancy of last resort.
- Ironically, more automation requires *better*-trained pilots, not less-trained ones: overreliance on autopilots degrades manual flying skills, which is why regulators and airlines force pilots to keep hand-flying.
]

.pull-right-small[

### Two cautionary tales

**[Qantas Flight 72](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qantas_Flight_72) (2008)**: A faulty air-data computer fed corrupted data to the flight computers, which commanded two violent nosedives; over 100 were injured. The crew hand-flew the damaged A330 to a safe emergency landing.

**[Air France 447](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_France_Flight_447) (2009)**: Iced-over sensors made the autopilot quit mid-Atlantic. The startled crew, out of manual-flying practice, stalled a perfectly flyable A330; all 228 aboard died.
]



---
# Why learn how to code in the age of AI?

.pull-left-wide[

### A thought experiment

Would you board a plane operated by someone who just learned how to fly... by chatting with ChatGPT?

Probably not. But why not? The autopilot does most of the flying anyway, and the LLM gives great flying advice.

### What that means for you

- AI coding assistants, are great, but data science projects are not standardized, and you still have to do much more than just the takeoffs and landings.
- AI might fail you when things get difficult. If you can't "hand-fly" — read, reason about, and write code yourself — you won't even notice you're in trouble.
- Pilots are required to keep hand-flying for good reason. If you let AI do all the coding while you're still learning, the "brain muscles" you came here to train will not grow.
]

# AI use in and for the course (cont.)

.pull-left-vwide[

### Can AI tools (LLM-based coding assistants) be used for assignments?

- There is not much I can do to prevent you from using them.
- The Hertie School has a [guideline](https://hertieschool.sharepoint.com/sites/CurricularAffairs/Student%20%20facing%20files/Forms/AllItems.aspx?id=%2Fsites%2FCurricularAffairs%2FStudent%20%20facing%20files%2FAI%20Guidelines%20for%20Teachers%20and%20Students_2025.pdf&parent=%2Fsites%2FCurricularAffairs%2FStudent%20%20facing%20files) in place that address the use of AI tools in education installed .
- Some key elements from the guidelines:
  - "Students are required to include a Statement of Authorship and AI Use at the end of each written assignment (...), which states their authorship including the use of AI and the absence of plagiarism."
  - "[A]ll AI tools that have been used need to be specified in the Statement of Authorship."
  - "Students are responsible for factual errors and false references in their assignments,
even if these have been provided by AI tools that were properly disclosed. The assignment
will receive a grade penalty in such instances."
- "Non-disclosed or non-permitted (...) use of AI in assignments (...) is a
violation of good academic conduct."
]

# AI use in and for the course (cont.)

.pull-left-vwide[

### *Should* you use AI tools for this course?

- You are a student at one of the leading policy schools in the world. You decided to invest a considerable amount of time and money to learn about data science and public policy here. I think you're at the right place to do so.
- However, the learning is still on you. What is key is that you want to *understand* what you are doing. That will require you to think hard and work hard. And that is ultimately what you need to excel in a data-based job.
- Or, you could just rely on some commercial language model to do the hard work for you. If you do that, you will notice that the muscles you wanted to train will not grow.
- That is not to say that AI is not useful for coding. It is incredibly powerful. But it also often fails spectacularly. You need to understand what is going on under the hood to make it work for you.
- I am not here to discipline and punish. I have no interest in that. What I can do is provide you with an environment that facilitates learning and sets the right incentives. If you want to learn, I will help you. If you don't, I can't.

]
